# About

This report walks through the classification model trained to predict
whether `{python} USERNAME` owns a game on BoardGameGeek — what the
model learned, how the features relate to ownership, and how well it
performs on held-out data. The model uses only features observable at
release and never reads BGG community signals.

For the model's picks for new and upcoming games, see the companion
[Predictions Report](`{python} f"../{USERNAME_SLUG}.html"`).

{{< include _collection.qmd >}}

# Modeling

For each user we train a binary classifier whose target is whether the
user owns a given game. The training process examines historical games
and learns which features tend to co-occur with games a user owns.
Features are dummies indicating presence/absence of designers, artists,
publishers, plus continuous features for playing time, player counts,
and recommended minimum age.

::: {.callout-note}
The model only uses features observable at release. It does not consume
BGG community signals (average rating, weight, number of users rated)
so it can score upcoming games before the community has weighed in.
:::

## Feature Importance

```{python}
#| label: feature-importance-prep
#| include: false
fi_pdf = arts.feature_importance.to_pandas()
MODEL_KIND = model_kind(arts.registration)
# Shared x-axis range so the partial-effects tabs are directly
# comparable. Linear models get a symmetric range (signed coefficients);
# tree models get a one-sided range (non-negative importance).
_cmax = float(fi_pdf["value"].abs().max()) if len(fi_pdf) else 1.0
if MODEL_KIND == "tree":
    FI_RANGE = (0.0, _cmax)
else:
    FI_RANGE = (-_cmax, _cmax)
```

```{python}
#| label: feature-importance-margin-note
#| output: asis
print("::: {.column-margin}")
if MODEL_KIND == "tree":
    print(
        "Each bar shows how much the model relied on a feature when "
        "deciding whether the user owns a game. Bigger bars = more "
        "important. Tree models don't expose a sign — only magnitude."
    )
else:
    print(
        "Each bar indicates how much an individual feature pushes the "
        "model towards or away from predicting \"owned\". Positive "
        "features (bars to the right) increase the user's probability "
        "of owning a game; negative features decrease the user's "
        "probability."
    )
print(":::")
```

```{python}
#| label: feature-importance-prose
#| output: asis
if MODEL_KIND == "tree":
    print(
        "Beyond predictions, the model tells us *what* it learned. For "
        "a tree-based model (gradient-boosted trees, random forest) the "
        "importance score tells us how much each feature contributed to "
        "the model's split decisions. There's no signed direction — "
        "just relative magnitude."
    )
else:
    print(
        "Beyond predictions, the model tells us *what* it learned. For "
        "a penalized logistic regression the coefficients tell us, for "
        "each feature, how much it shifts the user's probability "
        "(technically, the log-odds) of owning a game."
    )
```

```{python}
#| label: feature-importance
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: 100%
plot_feature_importance(
    fi_pdf,
    top_pos=15,
    top_neg=15,
    interactive=False,
    title="Feature importance",
    value_range=FI_RANGE,
    kind=MODEL_KIND,
)
```

## Top Games in Training

::: {.column-margin}
A user's model is trained by learning how *features* of games (mechanics, categories, playing time) relate to a user's probability of owning a game. 
:::

The highest-scored games from the training (out-of-fold) split. "Owned"
is the actual label (whether the user owns this game).

```{python}
#| label: top-games-training-prep
#| include: false
oof_joined = (
    arts.oof_predictions
    .join(data.games.select(["game_id", "name", "year_published"]), on="game_id", how="left")
    .sort("proba", descending=True)
)
val_test_joined = (
    pl.concat(
        [arts.val_predictions, arts.test_predictions],
        how="diagonal_relaxed",
    )
    .join(data.games.select(["game_id", "name", "year_published"]), on="game_id", how="left")
    .sort("proba", descending=True)
)
```

```{python}
#| label: top-games-training
itables_show(
    format_eval_table(oof_joined, top_n=100),
    paging=True,
    pageLength=15,
    classes="display compact",
    columnDefs=[{"className": "dt-center", "targets": [0, 2]}],
    style="width: 100%",
    allow_html=True,
)
```

## Top Games in Testing

```{python}
#| label: top-games-val-test
itables_show(

## Top Games by Year

::: {.column-margin}
In evaluating a user's model, we can also ask, retroactively which games would it have identified as top picks for recent years?
:::

Side-by-side comparison of the model's top picks for each year. Cells
shaded blue are games the user actually owns (true positives).

```{python}
#| label: top-games-by-year
#| column: page-right
#| output: asis
all_eval = pl.concat(
    [arts.oof_predictions, arts.val_predictions, arts.test_predictions],
    how="diagonal_relaxed",
)
html = build_topn_by_year_html(all_eval, top_n_per_year=15, since_year=2015)
if html:
    print("```{=html}")
    print(html)
    print("```")
else:
    print("No predictions in the eval splits to display.\n")
```
